system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2166-09-06 20:07:00 to 2166-09-09 17:14:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, tracheostomy, and multiple airway reconstructions was admitted due to persistent dysphagia, odynophagia, and cough over several weeks. She reported difficulty swallowing solids, pain at the trach site, and liquids going down the wrong way. A chest X-ray showed no pneumonia. A barium swallow study revealed upper pharyngeal edema, gastroesophageal reflux reaching the pharynx, and a small hiatal hernia, but no tracheoesophageal fistula. She was managed with optimized reflux treatment, dietary modifications, and speech therapy guidance. A periapical abscess was noted and referred for dental follow-up. She improved clinically and was discharged with instructions for continued reflux management, soft diet, and outpatient follow-up.

Ms. ___ is a ___ year old woman with a trach secondary to 
tracheobronchomalacia from premature birth, s/p 4 airway 
reconstructions, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, chronic tracheitis 
and bronchitis on chronic suppresion, laryngeal and tracheal 
stenosis, who was last admitted ___ for airway montoring 
after ___ T-tube placement. She presented with increased 
trach site pain, discharge, and reproducible chest pain that 
started 1 day prior to admission. She had sufficient oxygen 
saturations without additional oxygen supplementation.

# Pain at trach site: Upon admission, the patient was seen by 
ENT and interventional pulmonology. Initially she was made NPO 
including medications. ENT did a fiberoptic laryngoscopy, and 
this showed no tracheitis or inflammation. She also reported 
some increased discomfort with swallowing, and a CT trachea was 
done, which showed no esophageal compression. Diet was resumed 
per previous speech and swallow assessment done on ___, because 
speech and swallow was not in house on the day of admission 
(Labor Day) to re-evaluate. Diet was as follows: thin liquids, 
regular solids. Sips in between bites. TID oral care. Speech and 
swallow did see her during her admission, said she looked the 
same as she did on ___, and agreed that she should continue on 
the aforementioned diet. Trach site/T-tube was managed per 
recommendations of IP: Mucinex ___ mg po bid q12h, 5cc NS to 
the t-tube bid, Suction via the t-tube bid, humidified air to 
the tracheostoma to help with crusting. During her last 
admission ___, she had been started on levofloxacin for 
tracheitis prophylaxis ___, to complete on ___. Team continued 
levofloxacin while inpatient.

Her pain was initially controlled with IV morphine, as oral pain 
medications were not effective. After about a day on IV pain 
control, she tolerated a transition to PO pain control with 
percocet. For discharge pain control regimen, the team reviewed 
PMP data, to ensure a safe discharge with an appropriate amount 
of opioids. She reported that she had oxycodone and liquid 
tylenol at home from her last admission, and that she would take 
this for pain control.

# Lightheadedness: On admission patient was complaining of 
lightheadness, that improved with IVF and increased PO intake. 
Likely was a result of poor PO intake because of pain. Team did 
not think it was result of hypoxia as patient's O2 stats 
remained stable and she was breathing comfortably. PO intake was 
encouraged, and her symptoms improved.

# Anemia: Patient was noted to have long standing microcytic 
anemia from lab review. H/h were stable inpatient and recommend 
an outpatient workup and follow up.

# Liver mass: As mentioned above, patient had a CT trachea done. 
On this CT, a hypodense right posterior liver mass found. The 
mass was stable from previous imaging, but will need outpatient 
follow-up. These findings were communicated by telephone to pt's 
PCP prior to discharge.

TRANSITIONAL ISSUES
#Day of discharge is final day of levofloxacin course started

question of consolidation on CT, but no change was made to her 
antibiotic treatment given the lack of clinical evidence of 
pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. I know you're here because of increased pain around your trach site and some chest discomfort. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The pain started yesterday. It’s right where the T-tube goes in. It hurts more when I swallow or move my neck. And my chest feels sore in the middle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or changes in your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Breathing is okay, but I’ve been avoiding eating because it hurts too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll get you some pain control. For now, we’re going to hold off on food and meds by mouth until ENT and pulmonology see you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I need my reflux meds. I get heartburn if I miss them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give your omeprazole through your feeding tube if needed. Your safety comes first. We’ll restart your diet as soon as we know it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ENT team did a laryngoscopy. They didn’t see any infection or inflammation in your trachea. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected? Why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. It could be irritation or granulation tissue. We’re ordering a CT scan of your trachea to look deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. There’s no sign of infection, fluid collection, or esophageal compression. The pain isn’t showing a clear cause on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s likely post-op pain from the T-tube site. We’ll restart your diet based on your last speech and swallow evaluation since they weren’t here yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that — thin liquids and regular solids, right? With sips in between bites?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And three times daily oral care. The speech team will see you later to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting IV morphine for your pain since your oral meds weren’t strong enough at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really struggling to eat because of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed you were a bit lightheaded on admission. That’s likely from not eating or drinking enough. We’re giving IV fluids and encouraging you to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less dizzy now. I had some apple juice and crackers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That’s exactly what we wanted to see. Your oxygen levels have stayed stable too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The speech and swallow team saw you. They say your swallowing looks the same as before. You can keep your current diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried I’d have to go back to pureed food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. We’re also continuing your levofloxacin. It was started during your last admission for tracheitis prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there an infection now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of active infection. But we’re finishing the course as planned. Better safe than sorry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is doing better with the IV meds. We’d like to switch you to oral Percocet to see if that controls it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used oxycodone before. Will that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We checked your prescription history. You can use the oxycodone and liquid Tylenol you have at home for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oral meds are helping. Pain is about a 3 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep monitoring. Also, your labs show you have a long-standing mild anemia. It hasn’t changed. You should follow up with your doctor after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable, so no emergency. But an outpatient workup is a good idea to understand the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — your CT showed a small 7 mm spot in your liver. It’s unchanged from before, so likely not serious. But your PCP should follow it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A liver spot? Is it cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. It’s stable, which is reassuring. But we always check these things over time. Your doctor will monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is controlled, you’re eating and drinking, and your breathing is stable. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your secretions increase, change color, or smell bad, or if you get fevers, worsening pain, or trouble breathing — come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your reflux meds, stay on your current diet, and finish your antibiotics. And follow up for your anemia and liver spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, tracheostomy, and multiple airway reconstructions was admitted for increased trach site pain, chest discomfort, and reduced oral intake due to pain. She was initially managed with NPO status and IV pain control. ENT evaluation and CT trachea showed no infection, inflammation, or structural cause for pain. She resumed her prior diet after speech and swallow assessment confirmed safety. Pain was transitioned from IV morphine to oral oxycodone, with plans to continue home medications. Lightheadedness resolved with IV fluids and improved intake. Chronic microcytic anemia was noted and recommended for outpatient workup. A stable 7 mm liver hypodensity was identified on CT and communicated to her PCP. She improved clinically and was discharged home with instructions to monitor for worsening symptoms and complete follow-up for anemia and liver imaging.
